chain.g: rose (plant of the genus Rosa or its flower)

ety.text: From Middle English rose, roose, from Old English rōse, but with its vowel influenced by Old French rose, both from Latin rosa. cognates and more remote and uncertain etymology The Latin is of uncertain origin, but likely via Oscan from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) (Aeolic ϝρόδον (wródon)), from Old Persian *vr̥dah (“flower”) (compare Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬜𐬀- (var^əδa-), Sogdian [script needed] (ward), Parthian wâr, late Middle Persian [Term?] (gwl /⁠gul⁠/), Persian گل (gol, “rose, flower”), and Middle Iranian borrowings including Old Armenian վարդ (vard, “rose”), Aramaic וַרְדָּא (wardā) / ܘܪܕ…

senses.d: A shrub of the genus Rosa, with red, pink, white or yellow flowers.
A flower of the rose plant.
ex:
1794, Robert Burns, "A Red, Red Rose:"
O my Luve's like a red, red rose
That's newly sprung in june...
Rose is a rose is a rose is a rose.

senses.d: A plant or species in the rose family. (Rosaceae)
Something resembling a rose flower, such as a compass rose.
A bouquet of circles.
The rose flower, usually depicted with five petals, five barbs, and a circular seed.
A nontraditional tincture in Canadian heraldry, corresponding to pink.
A purplish-red or pink color, the color of some rose flowers.
A round nozzle for a sprinkling can or hose.
The usually circular base of a light socket in the ceiling, from which the fitting or chandelier is suspended.
To make rose-colored; to redden or flush.
ex: A maid yet rosed over with the virgin crimson of modesty.

senses.d: To perfume, as with roses.
ex:
the very nape of her white neck
Was rosed with indignation

senses.d: Having a purplish-red or pink color; rosy.

grp.label: a plant or species in the rose family (Rosaceae)

ety.text: From Old Spanish rosa, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin rosa (the expected inherited form would be *ruesa).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rosa, from Latin rosa (“rose”). Senses referring to the color are an ellipsis of cor-de-rosa. Compare French rose.
Inherited from Old French rosier. Equivalent to rose + -ier.
From rosa + -al.
From Latin rosāria, from rosārium (“rose-garden”) or from rosa (“rose”) + -eira.
From rosa (“rose”) + -ato.
Inherited from Old Spanish rosado, borrowed from Latin rosātus.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French pomme, from Old French pome, from Latin pōma, plural of pōmum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular, from Proto-Italic *poomos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”). Compare English pome.
Inherited from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

Inherited from Old Spanish alcarchofa, from Andalusian Arabic الخرشوفة (al-ḵaršúfa), from Arabic الخُرْشُوف (al-ḵuršūf, “artichoke”). Compare Portuguese alcachofra and Catalan carxofa. Related to English artichoke.
From Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cribum, dissimilated form of Latin cribrum attested in some late glosses.

From Middle English rosmary, rosemarye, alteration (based on rose + Mary) of earlier Middle English rosmarine, rosemaryn, partly from Old French rosmarin, partly directly from Latin rōsmarīnus (“rosemary”), from rōs (“dew, moisture”) + marīnus (“marine, of the sea”). Displaced native Old English boþen.

senses.d: A shrub, Salvia rosmarinus (formerly Rosmarinus officinalis), that originates from Europe and Asia Minor and produces a fragrant herb used in cooking and perfumes.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin rōsmarīnus.
Inherited from Latin rosmarīnus.
Borrowed from Late Latin Rōmaeus, from Byzantine Greek ῥωμαῖος (rhōmaîos, literally “Roman”), a sobriquet given to Roman Catholic pilgrims to the Holy Land.
Borrowed from Arabic اَلإِكْلِيل (al-ʔiklīl), ellipsis of إِكْلِيل الْجَبَل (ʔiklīl al-jabal, “rosemary”).
Borrowed from Dutch rooster (“gridiron, table, list”), from Middle Dutch roosten (“to roast”). More at roast.

senses.d: A list of individuals or groups, usually for an organization of some kind such as military officers and enlisted personnel enrolled in a particular unit; a muster roll; a sports team, with the names of players who are eligible to be placed in the lineup for a particular game; or a list of students officially enrolled in a school or class.
ex: I'm number 12 on the roster for tonight's game.

senses.d: A list of the jobs to be performed by members of an organization and often with the date and time that they are expected to perform them.
ex: The secretary has produced a new cleaning roster for the Church over the remainder of the year.

senses.d: A schedule or timetable setting out shift times and dates for each employee of a business.
ex: Before uni starts check your work roster with your uni schedule to make sure there are no clashes with your classes.

senses.d: A bracketed list that shows the elements of a set.
To place the name of (a person) on a roster.
ex: I have rostered you for cleaning duties on the first Monday of each month.
New York Central rostered literally hundreds of engine subclassifications in contrast to the Spartan simplicity of Pennsy's ranks.

senses.d: To show the elements of a set by listing them inside brackets.
